reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Scalable S Q L with Spark and Microsoft Fabric
slides.transcript:
Welcome to Module 13, Scalable S Q L with Spark and Microsoft Fabric.

Before we move into Spark, think about what you already know. You have learned how to organize relational data, write S Q L queries, join tables, clean messy values, reshape data, use advanced analytical functions, and create reusable database views. Those ideas do not disappear when the data becomes larger.

[tts-break]

What changes is the computing environment. Spark can divide a large job across multiple workers. That gives us more computing power, but it also creates new questions. How is the data divided? When does data have to move between workers? Which operations create expensive shuffles? And when is Spark actually a better choice than a database?

The goal of this module is not to turn you into a Spark administrator. The goal is to help you carry your existing data-preparation skills into a distributed environment while keeping the same habits: know the grain, understand the schema, handle null values carefully, validate the output, and explain what the pipeline is doing.

slides.title: Same ideas, different environment
slides.transcript:
Spark S Q L does not erase the S Q L ideas we already learned. Filters, joins, grouping, windows, null handling, and row grain still matter.

[tts-break]

What changes is the execution environment. In Postgres, we usually think about one database engine managing tables and indexes. In Spark, the work may run across many workers and many data partitions. That means a correct query can still be expensive if it scans too much data or causes large shuffles.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you should be able to explain when distributed processing is useful, describe the basic Spark execution model, and understand how Spark S Q L and data frames connect. You should also be able to reason about lakehouse tables, schema choices, Delta tables, query plans, partitions, and shuffles at an introductory level. The goal is practical understanding, not cluster administration.

slides.title: Roadmap
slides.transcript:
We will start by asking why a workload might need distributed processing. Then we will introduce the Spark execution model. After that, we will connect S Q L and data frames, discuss lakehouse and Delta concepts, and practice familiar S Q L patterns.

[tts-break]

The last part of the module focuses on query plans, partitions, shuffles, and project-style reasoning.

slides.title: Spark is not just bigger Postgres
slides.transcript:
It is tempting to think of Spark as simply a larger version of Postgres. That is not a good mental model.

Postgres is a database system. It is designed to store and manage relational data, support transactions, enforce constraints, use indexes, and answer database queries efficiently.

[tts-break]

Spark is mainly a distributed computing engine. Its strength is processing large analytical workloads by spreading work across multiple machines or workers.

In a real organization, these tools can work together. A database may manage operational data, while Spark prepares large analytical datasets. The question is not which tool is better in general. The question is which tool fits the workload.

slides.title: When a database may be better
slides.transcript:
Spark is not always the right tool. A conventional database may be better for transactional workloads, frequent small updates, low-latency point lookups, and strict relational constraints.

If the data fits comfortably in the database and the query workload is already efficient, moving to Spark may add complexity without much benefit.

slides.title: When Spark may be better
slides.transcript:
Spark becomes useful when data and computation benefit from being divided across workers. Large file-based transformations, broad scans, batch feature preparation, and analytical pipelines across different storage systems are common examples.

The main benefit is parallelism, but parallelism also introduces new costs such as coordination and shuffling.

slides.title: Distributed vocabulary
slides.transcript:
There are four Spark terms I want you to recognize.

A partition is one piece of a larger dataset. A task is a unit of work that processes a partition. A stage is a group of tasks that can run before Spark needs to reorganize the data. A shuffle is the movement of data between workers.

Here is the key idea. Parallel processing is helpful when workers can operate on separate pieces of data. It becomes more expensive when the workers must exchange large amounts of data. That is why the word shuffle will come up repeatedly in this module.

slides.title: Driver and executors
slides.transcript:
A Spark application usually has a driver and one or more executors.

Think of the driver as the coordinator. It understands the job, builds the execution plan, and coordinates the work. Think of the executors as the workers. They process partitions of the data and perform the tasks assigned to them.

[tts-break]

Suppose we have a very large sales dataset. Instead of one process reading every row, Spark can divide the data into partitions and let several executors work at the same time.

One important warning is that we normally do not want to bring a huge distributed dataset back to the driver. Doing that can create a memory bottleneck and defeats the purpose of distributing the work.

slides.title: S Q L to distributed plan
slides.transcript:
When you submit Spark S Q L, Spark does not simply read the statement from top to bottom and execute each word immediately.

It first understands the query and builds a logical plan. Then it optimizes that plan and produces a physical execution plan.

The physical plan may include table or file scans, filters, joins, aggregations, sorting, and data exchanges. An exchange is often a clue that data needs to move between workers.

You do not need to memorize the entire optimizer. The useful habit is to remember that your S Q L is translated into an execution plan, and that plan helps explain why one query may be much more expensive than another.

slides.title: Lazy evaluation
slides.transcript:
Spark often uses lazy evaluation.

That means many transformation steps describe what should happen without immediately processing the entire dataset. You might select a few columns, add a filter, and define another transformation. Spark can keep building the plan.

[tts-break]

The larger computation begins when an action needs an actual result. For example, displaying rows, counting records, collecting data, or writing a table can trigger execution.

This is useful because Spark can examine several transformations together and optimize the combined work before running it. So when you write Spark code, remember that defining a transformation and actually executing the job are not always the same moment.

slides.title: Spark S Q L and Data Frames
slides.transcript:
Spark gives us more than one way to express structured data transformations.

We can use Spark S Q L, which feels familiar if you already know S Q L. We can also use the data frame A P I, where transformations are written as code.

[tts-break]

These are not two completely separate worlds. Both can use Spark's structured processing engine.

For this course, Spark S Q L is a good bridge because you can focus on concepts you already understand: selecting columns, filtering rows, joining data, grouping values, and using window functions. Then, when you see the same operation written with a data frame, you can connect the code back to the S Q L idea.

slides.title: Temp views
slides.transcript:
A common notebook workflow is to load data into a data frame and then register that data frame as a temporary view.

Once the temporary view exists, we can query it with Spark S Q L.

The word temporary is important. This is not the same as a permanent database view from Module 12. A temporary Spark view usually belongs to the current session or notebook workflow. It is a convenient bridge between the data frame A P I and S Q L.

slides.title: Spark S Q L notebook example
slides.transcript:
The notebook example follows a simple sequence.

First, Spark reads a file into a data frame. Second, that data frame is registered as a temporary view. Third, Spark S Q L queries the temporary view.

Do not focus on memorizing every function call. Focus on the flow: file, data frame, temporary view, then S Q L.

This code requires a real Spark environment, so it is not intended to run inside the small browser S Q L practice engine used in the course.

slides.title: Fabric workflow
slides.transcript:
Microsoft Fabric gives us an environment where storage, notebooks, Spark, and analytical tables can work together.

A common workflow begins with files in a lakehouse. A notebook reads those files with Spark. We clean and transform the data, perhaps using both data frames and Spark S Q L. Then we save a curated result as a reusable table.

[tts-break]

Notice that the basic data-preparation process is still familiar. We inspect the source, define the grain, clean values, transform the structure, validate the result, and publish something useful. Fabric changes the environment, but it does not remove those responsibilities.

slides.title: Lakehouse layers
slides.transcript:
A lakehouse combines file storage with table-like access. Raw files may enter the lakehouse first. Curated outputs are often stored as Delta tables. Spark provides distributed compute over those data assets.

Reports, notebooks, and models consume the prepared results. This layered thinking helps keep raw, cleaned, and analytical data separate.

slides.title: Delta tables
slides.transcript:
Delta tables are important in many lakehouse workflows.

At a beginner level, think of a Delta table as data files with additional table-management information. Delta keeps a transaction log that records changes to the table and supports more reliable table operations than working with unrelated files alone.

[tts-break]

You do not need to learn every Delta feature here. The key idea is that curated lakehouse data can behave more like a managed table, which makes it easier to query, update, track, and reuse in analytical pipelines.

slides.title: Raw files versus managed tables
slides.transcript:
A raw file is flexible, but Spark may need to infer or be given the schema. A curated Delta table has a stronger table contract.

For teaching, think of raw files as ingestion material and tables as reusable analytical assets. That is not an absolute rule, but it is a helpful workflow.

slides.title: Schema inference caution
slides.transcript:
Spark can inspect a file and try to infer the schema. That is convenient when we are exploring data, but inference is still a guess.

A column that looks numeric may actually be an identifier. A date may be interpreted as plain text. A mostly empty column may be assigned an unexpected type.

For important pipelines, an explicit schema is often safer. It documents what each column is expected to contain and reduces the chance that the same file is interpreted differently later.

slides.title: Explicit schema example
slides.transcript:
The code on this slide defines an explicit schema in Pie Spark.

Rather than asking Spark to guess every data type, we tell it the expected column names and types in advance.

This takes more work than automatic inference, but it gives us a clearer contract. For example, we can intentionally store an identifier as text even if every current value happens to contain digits.

The larger lesson is the same one we used throughout the course: when the meaning is known, make the data type intentional rather than accidental.

slides.title: Portable S Q L lab
slides.transcript:
This deck includes a portable S Q L practice engine in the browser. It is not a Spark cluster. We use it to practice the relational logic that will transfer to Spark S Q L, such as grouping, joins, windows, and grain checks.

Spark-specific file reading and Delta operations should be run in Fabric or another Spark environment.

slides.title: Practice data
slides.transcript:
The browser practice database is intentionally small. It includes sales, admissions, survey responses, and web events.

These are not meant to be big-data examples. They are meant to help you practice S Q L logic before running the same kind of logic in Spark.

slides.title: Survey summary
slides.transcript:
Here we have a simple aggregate. The query groups survey responses by question and calculates the number of responses and the average score.

Run it in the browser and check the grain. One output row represents one question. In Spark S Q L, the same grouping idea would apply, but the data could be distributed across many partitions.

slides.title: Filter early
slides.transcript:
Filtering early can reduce unnecessary work.

Suppose a large sales table contains five years of history, but the analysis needs only the most recent month. If the filter can be applied before a large join or aggregation, Spark may have much less data to process.

[tts-break]

This does not mean we blindly move every filter to the beginning. The logic still has to remain correct. The principle is to remove data you know you do not need as early as the analytical logic safely allows.

slides.title: Group sales by product
slides.transcript:
This query groups order rows by product. The output grain changes from one order row to one product.

That grain change is important in Postgres and in Spark. In Spark, group by can also create a shuffle because rows with the same product may need to be brought together across workers.

slides.title: Join mindset
slides.transcript:
Joins need extra attention in a distributed system.

First, the same relational rule still applies: confirm the join keys and understand the relationship between the tables. A one-to-many join can multiply rows whether you are using Postgres or Spark.

Second, Spark may need to move data between workers so matching keys can meet. That movement can be expensive.

Before a large join, ask three questions. Are the keys correct? Is the output grain controlled? And can either side be reduced safely before the join?

slides.title: Explain habit
slides.transcript:
Build the habit of using the explain command.

The exact plan format in Spark is different from the plan you may see in Postgres, but the purpose is similar. We want evidence about what the engine plans to do.

Look for scans, filters, joins, aggregations, sorting, and exchanges. In Spark, exchanges are especially interesting because they often indicate that data will be redistributed between workers.

You do not need to understand every line of the plan. Start by asking where the expensive movement and large scans may occur.

slides.title: Partitions
slides.transcript:
Partitions are one of the basic units of Spark parallelism.

Imagine a very large book divided into sections. Different workers can read different sections at the same time. In Spark, partitions give executors pieces of the dataset that can be processed in parallel.

[tts-break]

If there are too few partitions, we may not use the available workers effectively. If there are far too many tiny partitions, Spark spends more time coordinating small tasks.

At this stage, you do not need to tune partition counts perfectly. I want you to understand why partitioning affects both parallelism and overhead.

slides.title: Partition pruning
slides.transcript:
Partition pruning can help Spark avoid reading data that is not relevant to the query.

Suppose a large table is organized by service date, and the query asks for only one month. If the storage layout supports it, Spark may skip partitions outside that month.

That can be much more efficient than scanning the entire dataset and then discarding most of the rows.

A partition column should match useful access patterns. A nearly unique identifier is often a poor choice because it can create too many tiny partitions.

slides.title: Column pruning
slides.transcript:
Column pruning is the column version of the same idea.

If a dataset has one hundred columns but your transformation needs only five, a columnar format can often avoid reading the other ninety-five.

This is one reason I do not want you to develop the habit of always selecting every column. During quick exploration, selecting all columns may be convenient. In a large production transformation, choose the columns you actually need.

slides.title: Shuffle
slides.transcript:
A shuffle means Spark has to redistribute data between workers.

Consider grouping millions of sales records by customer. The records for one customer may currently be spread across many partitions. Before Spark can calculate that customer's total, those related records need to be brought together.

[tts-break]

That movement uses network, memory, and sometimes disk resources. Grouping, global sorting, distinct operations, and many joins can cause shuffles.

A shuffle is not automatically a mistake. Sometimes it is required to answer the question. The goal is to recognize when it happens and avoid unnecessary movement.

slides.title: Group by and shuffle
slides.transcript:
Grouping is a good example of why distributed execution changes the performance discussion.

Logically, group by product is simple. We want all rows for the same product summarized together.

Physically, those product rows may be stored on different workers. Spark may need to redistribute them before the aggregation can finish.

So group by changes two things. It changes the row grain, and it may also create a data-movement cost.

slides.title: Join cost
slides.transcript:
The cost of a join depends partly on the size and distribution of the two inputs.

If both inputs are large, Spark may need to shuffle substantial amounts of data by the join key.

If one input is genuinely small, Spark may be able to broadcast that smaller table to the workers. Think of a small lookup table, such as a short list of department codes, being copied to the workers instead of moving the much larger fact table around.

[tts-break]

Do not assume a particular strategy will always be used. Filter unnecessary rows, choose only needed columns when it is safe, and inspect the execution plan to see what Spark actually intends to do.

slides.title: Order by caution
slides.transcript:
A global order by can be expensive because Spark must coordinate an ordering across the entire result.

That may be necessary for a final report or a small result that truly needs a global order. But many intermediate transformations do not require it.

Do not sort data simply because ordered output looks nicer while you are developing the pipeline. Sort when the order is part of the actual analytical requirement.

slides.title: Windows in Spark S Q L
slides.transcript:
The window-function ideas from Module 11 transfer directly to Spark S Q L.

Partition by defines which rows belong to the same analytical group. Order by defines the sequence inside that group. The lag function can retrieve a previous value. The function spelled L E A D can retrieve the next value. Window frames support running totals and moving calculations.

[tts-break]

The new consideration is execution cost. Window functions may require Spark to redistribute and sort data so the correct rows are together and in the correct order. The analytical idea is familiar, but the distributed engine has more work to coordinate.

slides.title: Readmission-style sequence
slides.transcript:
This example uses lag to compare an admission with the previous discharge for the same subject. The logic is the same kind of sequence analysis we used earlier.

In Spark, this window query may require sorting within each subject partition. Run the query and inspect the gap column.

slides.title: Null semantics still matter
slides.transcript:
Null values still mean what they meant earlier in the course.

A null value is not automatically zero. It is not the same as an empty string, and it is not the same as a placeholder such as unknown.

[tts-break]

This matters even more when a transformation is running across millions of rows. A small mistake in null handling can affect a very large output.

Keep the Module 9 habit: decide what missingness means, standardize it only when the business rule is clear, and validate the result.

slides.title: Dates and intervals
slides.transcript:
Temporal preparation remains important in Spark. Parse raw strings into typed dates or timestamps. Use Spark S Q L date functions appropriate to that environment.

And always state the output grain. For example, one row per event is different from one row per month.

slides.title: Common Table Expressions in Spark S Q L
slides.transcript:
Common table expressions are still useful in Spark S Q L. They make complex logic readable by separating stages.

The same rule from Module 11 applies: each stage should have a clear row meaning. In Spark, this also helps you reason about scans, filters, aggregations, and shuffles.

slides.title: Common Table Expression query example
slides.transcript:
This query uses common table expressions and a window function. The monthly sales stage has one row per month and product. The ranked stage keeps that grain and adds a rank within each month.

The final select keeps the top two rank groups. This is a good example of readable staged S Q L that can transfer to Spark S Q L.

slides.title: Creating a managed table
slides.transcript:
In a lakehouse workflow, we often save curated results as a table. This example creates a monthly sales table from raw sales data.

The important design choice is the output grain: one row per month and product. In a real Spark environment, you would also think about table format, location, and refresh process.

slides.title: Fabric S Q L surfaces
slides.transcript:
Microsoft Fabric has more than one place where S Q L can appear, so always check which engine is running your code.

A Spark notebook or Spark S Q L cell runs through Spark. A Fabric S Q L analytics endpoint uses a different S Q L serving environment and often follows T S Q L conventions.

[tts-break]

The same query concept may therefore need slightly different syntax depending on the surface.

When code fails, do not immediately assume the analytical idea is wrong. First ask: which engine am I using, and which S Q L dialect does that engine expect?

slides.title: Portability
slides.transcript:
A lot of S Q L knowledge transfers across Postgres and Spark S Q L, especially core relational patterns. But dialect differences remain.

Date functions, file-reading commands, table creation, and temporary view syntax can differ. A strong learner separates the relational idea from the engine-specific syntax used to express it.

slides.title: Reading files in Spark
slides.transcript:
Reading files is one place where Spark-specific code is very visible.

Spark can read C S V files, Parquet files, Delta data, and other formats. The exact read command depends on the format and environment.

After the file has been loaded into a data frame or a table, the relational logic becomes much more familiar. We can filter, join, group, reshape, and validate the data.

Keep the two stages separate in your mind. File ingestion brings the data into the processing environment. S Q L and data-frame transformations prepare it for analysis.

slides.title: Project overview
slides.transcript:
The project asks students to build a small Spark S Q L pipeline. First, inspect the source schema and grain. Second, clean and type the needed columns. Third, summarize monthly product revenue or readmission intervals.

Finally, validate output grain and totals. In Spark, validation is still essential because distributed execution can make mistakes expensive.

slides.title: Project step: inspect
slides.transcript:
The first project step is inspection.

In a Spark notebook, the print schema command helps you inspect column names and data types. A show command lets you look at sample rows. A count action can tell you how many records exist, but remember that counting a distributed dataset triggers computation.

Use these tools intentionally. Before you clean or aggregate anything, answer the same questions you have used throughout the course. What columns do I have? What types do they use? Are values missing? And what does one raw row represent?

slides.title: Project step: curate
slides.transcript:
The curated table should not just be a copy of the raw data. It should have useful types, deliberate columns, and a documented row grain.

For example, a monthly sales table may have one row per product and month. A readmission table may have one row per repeat admission.

slides.title: Project validation
slides.transcript:
Validation is still required in Spark. A distributed pipeline that finishes successfully can still produce the wrong result.

State the expected row grain. Compare totals when the measure is additive. Check row counts at important stages. Inspect unexpected null values. Confirm that joins did not multiply the data. And review the execution plan for unnecessarily large scans or shuffles.

[tts-break]

Think of validation as having two sides. First, is the result analytically correct? Second, is the pipeline doing the work in a reasonable way for the scale of the data?

A trustworthy pipeline should be both correct and explainable.

slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript:
Use this checkpoint to connect a requirement with the Spark concept that supports it.

Large files may benefit from distributed scanning. Grouping by a key may require a shuffle. A previous-event question suggests the lag function. A reusable curated lakehouse result may be stored as a Delta table. The explain command helps us inspect the execution plan.

The goal is not to memorize isolated vocabulary. It is to recognize which idea becomes relevant when the requirement changes.

slides.title: Assessment starter
slides.transcript:
The assessment starter asks for one row per product and month. The browser version is already complete so you can run it and inspect the result.

In a student assignment, you can remove part of the select or group by and ask students to finish it. After running it, explain the output grain and why a Spark version may need a shuffle for the grouping keys.

slides.title: Object decision guide
slides.transcript:
This decision guide helps you choose where work belongs. Transactional workflows often belong in a database. Large file transformations often fit Spark. Reusable lakehouse outputs often become Delta tables.

Small dashboard queries may fit a database or S Q L endpoint. Batch feature preparation may fit Spark. The best choice depends on workload, freshness, governance, and scale.

slides.title: Module 13 takeaways
slides.transcript:
These are the main habits from Module 13. Keep the relational thinking you built earlier. Add distributed cost awareness. Use raw files, temporary views, and Delta tables deliberately.

[tts-break]

Inspect plans. Validate outputs. And match the tool to the workload instead of assuming Spark is always better.

slides.title: Next: Module 14
slides.transcript:
Module 14 brings the course together.

It is important to be clear about one thing. Module 14 is a course synthesis and a sample data-preparation walkthrough. It is not the official final-project assignment. The actual project instructions, rubric, due date, required files, and submission details are in Canvas.

[tts-break]

In Module 14, we will connect the major habits from the entire course. We will start with source meaning and grain, then move through profiling, cleaning, integration, reshaping, validation, reusable outputs, and documentation.

Spark adds one more perspective to that workflow: sometimes the same data-preparation ideas need to operate at a much larger scale. But the core standard does not change. Understand the data, make deliberate transformations, validate what you produce, and be able to explain your decisions.
